extracted.intended_audience: aspiring literary writers, poets, and critics (young authors seeking craft and publication insight)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for literary writers (poets, novelists, essayists) drawn from anecdotal memoir about meetings with established authors, editors, and publishers; focuses on diction, authenticity, publication, and the effects of revision/proofing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction fidelity / resist archaisms for versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctor Holmes confessed that he had a prejudice against some words that he could not overcome; for instance, nothing could induce him to use 'neath for beneath, no exigency of versification or stress of rhyme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not sacrifice natural diction to meet a rhyme or metrical pressure; avoid archaisms or contracted forms if they jar with your voice or intention. The anti-pattern is forcing an archaic/contracted word ('neath') into a line just to rhyme or fit meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose words that carry meaning (but balance with musicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowell contended that he would use any word that carried his meaning; and I think he did this to the hurt of some of his earlier things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize words that convey the intended meaning, but be mindful of their effect on tone, sound, and overall music of the piece. Meaning alone can damage a poem's ear or style if not integrated with musical and tonal considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'too much literature' — favor naturalness over ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowell was then probably in the revolt against too much literature in literature, which every one is destined sooner or later to share; there was a certain roughness, very like crudeness, which he indulged before his thought and phrase mellowed to one music in his later work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of overwrought, self-conscious literary ornament. Early experiments in roughness or revolt against excessive decorum may precede maturation, but effective writing ultimately finds an integrated, natural music rather than showy 'literature for literature's sake.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Final wording is crucial — a single line can 'kill' a poem
rubrics_metrics.description: He agreed with me that it would kill the poem if it came out in that shape. He instantly set about repairing the mischief... the final reader had entered so sympathetically into the realistic intention of my poem as to contribute the modification which had nearly been my end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend carefully to exact wording; printing/proofing errors or ill-judged alterations can destroy a poem's effect. Vet final proofs and be vigilant about any last-minute changes, since small textual shifts may have large negative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreaders and editors should respect authorial intention
rubrics_metrics.description: The final reader had entered so sympathetically into the realistic intention of my poem as to contribute the modification which had nearly been my end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and proofreaders must avoid over-identifying with an author's perceived intention to the point of changing the work's tone or truth; sympathetic but misguided emendations can harm the piece. Conversely, authors should communicate intentions where necessary to prevent misread edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers evaluate both intrinsic quality and perceived reader reception
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can forecast the fortune of a new book, but he knew as well as any publisher can know not only whether a book was good, but whether the reader would think so; and I suppose that his house made as few bad guesses, along with their good ones, as any house that ever tried the uncertain temper of the public with its ventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing work for publication, consider both artistic merit and how readers are likely to receive it. Publishers often judge market perception as much as textual quality; writers should be aware of the audience dimension without compromising essential integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value frankness and honesty about authorship and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: I heard fames that I had accepted as proofs of power treated as factitious, and witnessed a frankness concerning authorship, far and near, that I had not dreamed of authors using.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity in discussing writing, authorship, and reputation is valued; avoid inflated claims or reliance on contrived fames. An honest appraisal of a work's strengths and weaknesses promotes clearer criticism and better craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to universal human concerns to engage readers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is best to find that all men are of the same make, and that there are certain universal things which interest them as much as the supernal things, and amuse them even more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate universal human experiences and emotions — these resonate widely. While specificity is important, anchoring work in common human concerns helps readers connect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didacticism or posing as moral exemplar
rubrics_metrics.description: A defect of the Puritan quality ... they propose themselves to you as an example ... Hawthorne had nothing of this about him; he was no more tacitly than he was explicitly didactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for subtlety rather than overt moralizing. Readers respond better to works that illuminate rather than lecture; authenticity and portrayal of characters' complexity are preferable to authorial sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and lack of pose build trust and lasting esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing could have been further from the behavior of this very great man than any sort of posing ... he was as much abashed by our encounter as I was ... he made an absolute equality between us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate a genuine voice and comportment; affectation or self-conscious posing undermines the work and the author's rapport with readers and peers. Humility and sincerity are enduring virtues in literary reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings and closure matter (beware indefinite closes unless intentional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Everybody was reading it, and more or less bewailing its indefinite close, but yielding him that full honor and praise which a writer can hope for but once in his life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how a work's ending will be received; an unresolved or 'indefinite' close can frustrate readers unless it serves a clear artistic purpose. Even when forgiven for other strengths, an unsatisfactory ending is often a target of critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue and conversational tone: balance lightness with depth
rubrics_metrics.description: It was such talk ... It was as light and kind as it was deep and true, and it ranged over a hundred things ... with a perpetual sparkle ... and the constant glow of Lowell's incandescent sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for dialogue and narrative voice that can be both witty/light and intellectually substantial. A balance of genial surface charm and deeper, true insight makes for compelling writing and memorable conversational passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for unified musical phrasing — 'mellow to one music'
rubrics_metrics.description: There was a certain roughness ... before his thought and phrase mellowed to one music in his later work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a consistent tonal/musical identity in prose or poetry. Early experimentation may sound uneven; maturation produces a more integrated 'music'—seek cohesion in cadence, diction, and rhythm across a piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain independent critical judgment; avoid alliance with cliques
rubrics_metrics.description: He seemed willing that I should know they were not thought so very undying in Boston, and that I should not take the notion of a Mutual Admiration Society too seriously ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on group praise or literary cliques as the sole validation of work. Keep critical standards independent; be wary of accepting unexamined acclaim from a 'Mutual Admiration Society.'
